title: Constants and const-Qualified Objects
learningObjectives: Explain the central rules behind constants and const-qualified objects in C.
Identify the relevant types, declarations, operators or library facilities.
Trace a worked example and explain its result.
Recognize common mistakes, portability concerns and unsafe assumptions.
Apply the concept in a small program and test normal and boundary cases.

understand.concept: A constant expression is an expression that can be evaluated where the language requires a compile-time constant. The const qualifier makes an object non-modifiable through that lvalue; it does not automatically make every initialized object a compile-time constant expression in C. Enumeration constants and macros have different rules from const-qualified objects.
understand.whyItMatters: Clear constants reduce accidental changes and communicate intent. Knowing the distinction between const objects, macros and enumeration constants avoids assuming they have identical type, scope or evaluation behaviour.
understand.analogy: Think of a type as a contract that describes what kind of value an object can hold and which operations make sense for it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only an introduction; C types also determine representation, conversions, alignment and constraints.

explain.narrative:
A constant expression is an expression that can be evaluated where the language requires a compile-time constant. The const qualifier makes an object non-modifiable through that lvalue; it does not automatically make every initialized object a compile-time constant expression in C. Enumeration constants and macros have different rules from const-qualified objects.

Clear constants reduce accidental changes and communicate intent. Knowing the distinction between const objects, macros and enumeration constants avoids assuming they have identical type, scope or evaluation behaviour.

When reviewing code, identify the declared types first, then trace conversions and the exact expression being evaluated. Compile with warnings enabled and test boundary values. Do not rely on assumptions about another compiler or machine.

practise.guidedTask: Define configuration values using const objects, an enum constant and a macro. Explain their types, scope and when each is suitable.
practise.independentTask: Refactor repeated literal values into named constants. Keep buffer capacities, protocol values and mutable state clearly distinguished.
hints: const prevents modification through the qualified lvalue; it is not a universal compile-time constant marker.
Macros are handled by the preprocessor and have no ordinary C type.
Initialize const objects at declaration where possible.
Use names that communicate units and constraints.
